transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-28
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Kapoor (KairoTech CTO), Elena Petrova (Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (DevOps)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, i'm maya with Redwood, AE on this account. diego is our solutions engineer. could you run through a little about what you're building, ravi?

[00:18] Ravi: sure yeah, um so KairoTech we run a multi-tenant customer support layer for some fintech partners. We're exploring adding an LLM assistant for ticket triage, summarization, and a customer-facing chat that can create tickets. latency is important for chat flows but we also need to keep inference costs reasonable.

[00:35] Elena: hi, yes. technical constraints: about 10k peak daily users, roughly 2-3M tokens/day expected once in prod. We expect a mixed-language footprint: EN, ES, PT-BR, and occasional FR and DE. We also have very long context needs for full conversation history + knowledge snippets—some cases 20k-30k tokens of context.

[00:55] Diego: okay, that's helpful. so two big axes: long context and multilingual. have you evaluated any models so far?

[01:05] Ravi: we've tried some hosted APIs, openai for quick prototyping and a small play with local Mistral and Llama 3, but haven't done a serious cost or latency benchmark. our legal team is pushing for data residency and more control over PII flows—so dedicated or private is on the table.

[01:25] Maya: perfect. today we'll cover model selection tradeoffs, how Redwood routes and can fallback between variants, and deployment modes. also we'll talk about tool-calling patterns—retrieval, ticket-API, and any DB writes.

[01:40] Diego: quick note: when you say 20k-30k tokens context, do you mean sliding window across the entire convo + KB snippets, or single turn context?

[01:50] Elena: mostly single-turn context because we stitch convo history + retrieval snippets into the prompt for high-fidelity summaries. so yes, a single prompt can hit 25k tokens.

[02:05] Diego: got it. in that case, options are: use a 32k-context open model (where available), or use long-context strategies—prefix KV caching, retrieval-augmented approaches where you summarize older parts, or windowed stitching. Redwood supports automatic KV caching and prefix caching to reduce repeated tokens; but for extremely long single prompts, you need a model with a native long context or offload context retrieval.

[02:30] Ravi: can you run through model families? we need to weight cost and hallucination risk.

[02:36] Diego: sure. quick high-level: Llama-family variants (Llama 3 derivs) are cost-efficient and good for instruction-following with quantization, but may need fine-tuning for safety. Mistral tends to be strong on instruction tasks and smaller footprint. Falcon gives strong reasoning for some workloads but can be heavier. MPT has opt-in conversation-level performance; tokenization differs per family which affects multilingual. Redwood maintains perf profiles — some models have known 32k wide context builds, some 16k. We can recommend quantized 4-bit models to reduce cost on Dedicated.

[03:05] Elena: tokenization question: how much does tokenization impact our 32k needs for Portuguese/Spanish?

[03:12] Diego: quite a bit. languages with compounds or accents can expand token counts depending on the tokenizer. we suggest sending a sample of your top 50 customer prompts in the target languages; we'll run a tokenization analysis and show expected tokens per model family.

[03:28] Ravi: noted. on tool-calling—our plan is: retrieval from internal vector DB, then a call to our ticketing API to open a ticket with structured fields. we also want the assistant to be able to run a small SQL query for account lookup. any security concerns?

[03:45] Maya: standard patterns: separate tool-invocation layer, strong RBAC for who can trigger writes, and audit logs for any outbound API calls. in private/dedicated deployments we offer VPC peering and optional customer-managed egress. KMS for keys, HSM for extra assurance. Diego can go into tracing and observability.

[04:05] Diego: from an ops perspective, Redwood supports function/tool calling patterns (we've seen some parity with FaaS connectors). we recommend: (1) retrieval results should be scored and truncated, (2) only pass minimal structured context for write actions, and (3) use signature checks or intent-confirmation steps before executing DB writes. for ticket creation, a two-step confirm with the user helps reduce erroneous writes.

[04:35] Elena: okay cool. what about latency—if we use a 32k model on Dedicated, are we looking at 2-3x the per-token latency vs 16k small models?

[04:45] Diego: yeah long-context models typically have higher per-token latency and memory pressure; but dedicated GPUs and batching strategy matter. Redwood Dedicated gives predictable throughput and we can provision specific GPU types for those long context cases. we can also use hybrid: route strict low-latency short-turn traffic to a smaller 16k model hosted, and long-context heavy requests to dedicated long-context instances. Redwood routing supports policy-based routing and automatic fallback.

[05:10] Ravi: our teams want predictable latency for SLAs—preferably p95 under 600ms for interactive flows. is that feasible?

[05:18] Diego: feasible for short-turns on a hosted fast tier. For long-turns with 30k prompt, 600ms is unrealistic unless you heavily cache or summarize. we should map which flows require interactive SLA vs background tasks, and then architect accordingly.

[05:35] Maya: across customers we do mixed routing often: chat actions go to fast hosted variant; heavy summarization goes to dedicated pools with longer SLOs. Do you have internal classification of interactive vs batch?

[05:45] Elena: yes, we can flag critical flows in the prompt metadata. We'll share that in the POC.

[05:50] Ravi: data residency—our finance partners require EU-only processing for EU customers. can Redwood support region pinning?

[05:58] Maya: yes, Redwood supports region pinning on Dedicated and Private. Hosted can be region-restricted where available. For Private, you can run the control plane in your VPC or on-prem with customer-managed networking, KMS integration, and audit logs.

[06:12] Samir: on the private deployment, what's the maintenance/ops lift? will your team handle upgrades?

[06:18] Maya: for private we offer a deployment package; customers own infra, Redwood supports orchestration and optional managed upgrades under an enterprise agreement. Dedicated is our middle-ground—Redwood manages infra but you get reserved GPU pools and isolation.

[06:32] Diego: to add—quantization and kernel selection matter a lot for cost. on Dedicated, we can test int8/4-bit profiles and choose kernels that reduce latency. We'll provide suggested quant profiles for each model in the benchmark report.

[06:48] Elena: are there any models you wouldn't recommend for our multilingual, regulated workflow?

[06:55] Diego: models without robust multilingual tokenizers or those with inconsistent hallucination patterns—some smaller family variants can be risky for customer-facing text. Also models without a long-context build will force you into complex prompt engineering. We'll call out model maturity and production readiness in our recommendation.

[07:15] Ravi: licensing—some open models have commercial restrictions. do you help with license review?

[07:22] Maya: yes we surface license info in the model catalog and flag commercial-use restrictions. for enterprise customers we can help coordinate legal reviews and provide proof-of-origin where required.

[07:35] Diego: quick demo idea for POC: run the same prompt set against a 16k Llama variant, a 32k Mistral long-context build, and a quantized Falcon on a dedicated pool. Compare latency, cost per 1k tokens, and output quality on our eval rubric.

[07:55] Elena: that sounds ideal. we want to include Spanish and Portuguese in the eval. also include a few edge cases that cause hallucinations.

[08:10] Maya: perfect. we'll need sample prompts and data. elena, you said top 50 prompts and token distribution?

[08:18] Elena: yes, i'll assemble them—mix of short chat turns, long-summary cases, and ticket-creation flows. we'll obfuscate any PII.

[08:28] Samir: security asks: SOC2 report, SAML SSO, RBAC controls, audit log format, and KMS integration. we also need an exportable audit trail for regulators.

[08:40] Maya: we'll share SOC2 docs and our SSO/RBAC guides. Dedicated and Private both have audit log options; Private gives you the most control. we'll attach a sample audit log schema and the KMS integration guide.

[08:55] Ravi: another thing—cost predictability. our finance team hates per-token surprises. can Redwood provide committed capacity or reserved pricing?

[09:05] Maya: yes, that's Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity. you commit to a monthly pool and we give discounted unit rates and predictable throughput. For Hosted we offer tiered volume discounts and quotas.

[09:20] Diego: technical note: secondary fallbacks—if long-context pool is saturated we can automatically fall back to shorter-context model with a preface explaining the limitation, or queue for background processing depending on your policy. this avoids hard failures.

[09:40] Elena: how do we instrument quality regressions after model updates? we need alerting when a model change causes drop in accuracy or unwanted responses.

[09:50] Diego: Redwood Optimize ties model rollouts to eval sets and alerting. you can pin model versions per route and run A/Bs with automatic rollback if eval metrics cross a threshold. we'll demo rollout controls in the POC.

[10:05] Ravi: ok this is super helpful. anything around translation quality—should we do an explicit translate-then-run or a single multilingual model?

[10:15] Diego: single multilingual models generally reduce latency and complexity, but if you have high-quality specialized translation requirements, you can chain a translation step. we'll evaluate both approaches in the benchmark. translation adds cost and latency though.

[10:30] Maya: wrap-up—so next steps: we'll send the pricing and deployment comparison doc, diego will send benchmark template, elena will share prompts and token distribution, samir will send security/reg requirements. then we schedule the POC kickoff.

[10:46] Ravi: timeline from our end: if benchmarks look good, we want a 6-week POC with clear success criteria—reduce manual triage by 30% and maintain p95 chat latency under 800ms for interactive flows.

[10:58] Maya: sounds reasonable. we'll put those success criteria into the POC brief. any final questions?

[11:06] Elena: one last: do you have examples of similar fintech customers who used private deployments for PCI-sensitive workflows?

[11:12] Maya: yes we have a case study—we'll share a redacted example and contact references under NDA.

[11:20] Samir: ok thanks everyone.

[11:22] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with the materials. bye.

Meeting end: 14:52 PDT
